The yield is the return an investor earns at that price, and a yield above 15% is the market's way of saying it expects trouble, or at least wants to be paid handsomely for the possibility of it.

For context, the latest official data show the 10-year Treasury at 5.21% and the 2-year at 4.79%. Those are the rates for lending to the US government, which is considered the safest borrower available. So CoreWeave's 15% is roughly ten percentage points above the risk-free benchmark. Translation: lenders see a large gap between the government's promise to repay and CoreWeave's, and they want ten points of compensation for the difference.

The bonds are not the only warning light. Investing.com reported that AI credit jitters pushed US tech default insurance to record highs. That insurance is called credit default swaps, which are contracts that pay out if a borrower fails to repay. Translation: investors are paying more than ever for protection against tech companies not paying their debts, which is an unusual thing to do when everyone says the sector is the future.

The mechanism is not mysterious. AI infrastructure is expensive, so companies borrow heavily to buy chips and build data centers before the revenue arrives. That works while lenders believe the revenue will arrive. When lenders begin to doubt it, the price of borrowing rises, which makes the buildout costlier, which makes the revenue harder to reach. It is a loop, and one that economists describe in several less cheerful ways.

The wider economic backdrop does not help. The Fed funds rate stands at 3.88%, inflation at 4.02% and unemployment at 4.2%, according to the latest official data. Long-term borrowing costs sit well above the central bank's policy rate, so companies that need years of cheap money to make the math work are not receiving it.

The sources provided do not say whether CoreWeave faces any imminent repayment problem, and a falling bond price is not a default. But the market has put a number on its worry, and that number is 15%. What to watch next is whether other AI borrowers see their bonds fall too, or whether CoreWeave is simply the first to be asked for a receipt.

articles.headline: Treasury Tells IMF to Check Its Forecasts, Then Bets $40 Trillion Debt on Growth Forecast
articles.dek: A new Treasury counselor dismissed the IMF's debt warning as 'messy' forecasting, while the deficit nears $2 trillion and the 10-year yield tops 5%.
articles.catch_up: The IMF's Kristalina Georgieva warned in Bangkok that strong U.S. growth alone cannot stabilize rising federal debt, which passed $40 trillion this year. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the country can 'grow our way out,' and his new counselor, David Zervos, answered the IMF on Thursday.
articles.why_it_matters: Higher Treasury yields feed directly into mortgage rates, which are around 7.5%, and make the government's own borrowing costlier. With divided government expected after the midterms, a fix for the deficit looks years away.
body: David Zervos, the newly appointed counselor to the Treasury Secretary, told CNBC on Thursday that the International Monetary Fund should remember 'how messy their forecasts have been' before commenting on U.S. debt. He was responding to IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, who said in Bangkok that strong American growth would not be enough to put federal debt on a sustainable path. It is a robust defense of the U.S. fiscal position, in the sense that it does not mention the U.S. fiscal position.

Zervos, a former chief market strategist at Jefferies, offered a list of IMF misses: a 2008 outlook with world growth at 3% before a global contraction, optimism on Southeast Asia before 1997, gloom on Russia in 2022, and optimism on Argentina after a $57 billion bailout. His conclusion was to 'take it all with a grain of salt.' Translation: the referee has made bad calls before, so the foul count should be disregarded.

The numbers the IMF was commenting on are not in dispute. CNBC's analysis says the fiscal 2026 deficit will land near $2 trillion, with the Congressional Budget Office estimating $1.993 trillion, or roughly 6.0% to 6.2% of GDP. Bessent has argued for a deficit below 4% of GDP by the end of President Trump's term, and CNBC says there is almost no way that happens.

The cost of that borrowing is already showing up. The 10-year Treasury yield, which was 5.21% in the latest official data, has climbed 123 basis points since the end of February. Translation: a basis point is a hundredth of a percentage point, so the government and everyone who borrows against its rates now pay about 1.23 points more. The 30-year mortgage hovers near 7.5%, and Redfin reported that pending home sales fell 4% in September, the biggest monthly drop in three years.

CNBC cites several causes: the war with Iran that began Feb. 28, which pushed up oil and diesel and raised the odds that the Federal Reserve hikes; heavy government bond issuance; and corporations borrowing hundreds of billions to build AI infrastructure. Treasuries are therefore competing for investors' money with companies promising to build the future, which is also the thing Bessent hopes will rescue the budget.

That hope has a price tag. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget calculates that growth alone would need a decade of 7.2% growth to balance the budget. GDP growth for the second quarter was just revised up from 1.5% to 2.2%. Closing that gap would require what CNBC calls an almost unimaginable transformation of the economy.

Higher rates also make the arithmetic worse. The CBO estimates that rates a half-point above its forecast would add $1.9 trillion to 10-year deficits, and 1.5 points above would add $6 trillion. It expects the 10-year to average 4.3%, versus 5.3% at the time of CNBC's analysis. The IMF, for its part, has been telling France to 'get your house in order,' so the U.S. is not being singled out.

The politics are less encouraging. Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House in the Nov. 3 midterms, and Trump pledged $5,000 checks to every adult citizen if they swept. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next speaker, wants to reverse $1 trillion in healthcare cuts. CNBC notes that higher yields are also attracting buyers, so expensive borrowing is not yet a crisis. Watch whether the Treasury's official deficit figure arrives with a forecast attached.
